# Cloud SOC Detection Lab — Microsoft Sentinel

I deployed Microsoft Sentinel on Azure, collected Windows Security Events from a monitored Windows Server, wrote KQL detection rules, simulated a brute-force attack against my own VM, investigated the resulting incident, and documented the response.

*Self-directed lab project, October 2026. All activity was generated by me against infrastructure I owned; the environment was deleted afterward.*

## Skills demonstrated

Microsoft Sentinel · Microsoft Defender portal · KQL · Azure Monitor Agent & data collection rules · Windows Security event analysis · detection engineering & rule tuning · MITRE ATT&CK (T1110, T1098) · incident response (NIST SP 800-61)

## Architecture

```
vm-endpoint (Windows Server 2022, Azure)
   │  Windows Security Events (all events)
   ▼
Azure Monitor Agent  ──  data collection rule: dcr-vm-endpoint
   │
   ▼
Log Analytics workspace: law-soc-lab
   │
   ▼
Microsoft Sentinel (Defender portal)
   ├─ 3 scheduled analytics rules (KQL)
   └─ Incidents → investigation → resolution
```

## What I built

- A Log Analytics workspace with Microsoft Sentinel, collecting Windows Security Events from a Windows Server 2022 VM through the Azure Monitor Agent
- Three scheduled analytics rules: brute force, successful logon after brute force, and privileged group change
- A controlled brute-force simulation: 11 failed RDP logons, an account lockout, then one successful logon
- A full investigation of the resulting High-severity incident, closed as a benign positive

## Detections

| File | Detects | Severity | Event IDs |
|---|---|---|---|
| [rule1-bruteforce.kql](detections/rule1-bruteforce.kql) | 10+ failed logons to one account from one IP in 15 minutes | Medium | 4625 |
| [rule2-bruteforce-success.kql](detections/rule2-bruteforce-success.kql) | A successful logon during or shortly after a failure burst | High | 4625 → 4624 |
| [rule3-admin-group.kql](detections/rule3-admin-group.kql) | A user added to a security group (deployed) / privileged group (tuned) | Medium | 4728, 4732, 4756 |
| [incident-timeline.kql](hunting/incident-timeline.kql) | Investigation query that rebuilds the attack timeline | — | 4624, 4625, 4732, 4740 |

All three rules fired during the test.

## Investigation

The High-severity incident showed 11 failed logons to the local administrator account from one IP, an account lockout (EventID 4740), and then a successful logon from the same IP about 13 minutes later.

Full write-up: **[incident-report.md](incident-report.md)** — timeline, investigation questions, containment steps, and lessons learned.

## Detection-engineering findings

1. **A join on the full account name silently fails.** Failed logons were logged as `MicrosoftAccount\soclabadmin`, the success as `vm-endpoint\soclabadmin`. I rewrote Rule 2 to match on the username, and it fired.
2. **Duplicate incidents.** A 5-minute schedule with a 1-hour lookback re-alerted on the same events. Fixed with 1-hour alert suppression.
3. **One RDP sign-in = two success events** (LogonType 3 and 10), which created two High incidents for one logon.
4. **Rule 3 was too broad.** It fired on the automatic Users-group add when an account is created. The tuned version filters to privileged groups.

## What I learned

The biggest surprise was that a detection can look correct and still never fire: the same account was logged under two different names, so the original join could not match. Testing each rule against real events, not just checking that it saves, is what caught it. I also saw how quickly duplicate alerts pile up when the lookback window exceeds the schedule, which made alert fatigue feel real. Next time, I would add an alert-grouping strategy and restrict RDP with Just-in-Time access from the start.
